1️⃣2️⃣ Programs launched. From the Summer Design Program, which started with 13 principals and now serves 85 school teams a year, to The Malott Educator Fellowship, our newest program, our pilot efforts increase principal tenure, spark #innovation, and respond to leaders’ needs.

1️⃣0️⃣ Principal Engagement Surveys, inviting Chicago’s principals to share their perspectives and publishing the results to hold ourselves and our partners accountable. 

9️⃣ Non-interim Chicago Public Schools CEOs. I learned something different from each one of them, AND the shifts at the top reinforced my commitment to local leadership.

8️⃣ Principal Appreciation Campaigns. Throughout October, we united thousands of partners and school communities to show their #PrincipalPrideChi.

Nearly two decades (!) ago, I was emerging from a tough professional year. I took on a big project, and it *almost* went well. Then, it went *spectacularly* wrong. The follow-up meant a series of all-nighters (for real), an enormous fight with my then-boyfriend (now-husband…phew!), and what felt like maybe the end of my career in #education (at least to my young head and heart).

What got me through? 

A smart, capable, hilarious group of (mostly) women who helped me clean up the mess, who helped me smooth over the fight, and who helped me find my next gig (and then the one after that). Women who reminded me that I was defined by more than one remarkably public failure. 

In honor of the moment and #WomensHistoryMonth, I am committed to owning my soft failures - in private and in public (like this!). I’m going to use each failure as an opportunity to know better, to do better, and to BE better. And I’m going to carry them up the U, believing in the future we are shaping together. 

One thing I learned from that early failure was to recognize my patterns. For example, I know I’m headed into a downtrend when:
⬇ Many of the #management systems and processes I rely on - at work and at home - stop working. 
⬇ My penchant for action, usually such an advantage, starts (and keeps) leading to unintended outcomes. 
⬇ My judgment is just… off. 
⬇ Even my words on a page - long my most reliable mechanism for processing and powering through - seem to lose their luster. 

Of course, when things start to spiral like that, I see my worst traits magnified, too. Traits like:
☑ My perfectionism.
☑ My tendency to micromanage.
☑ My ability to say the true things in the most unfair ways. 

Plenty of Harvard research shows that women my age are firmly in the tight spot when life seems to cost a lot, just as the priceless joys of adulthood start to wear off (see the picture!). Personally, I know that I have officially entered the low point of the U. 

And yet, reflecting on the remarkable care so many people offered last year, I can see that the gap (at least for me) is much narrower than it sometimes feels. 

In honor of this month, I’m spending this weekend writing some thank you notes to fifteen of the women who are riding the U with me and whom I know I can count on even on the toughest days. I hope the notes will inspire them to thank a few of the women in their networks. 

Lila Leff, Amber Kleeschulte Richard, Melissa Zaikos, Amanda Perkins, Naya Bloom, Acasia Wilson Feinberg, Melinda Wright, Heather Harding, Chaula Gupta, Phyllis Lockett, Janice Jackson, Sonya Anderson, Anna Alvarado, Elizabeth Alvarez, and Linda Erlinger… you’ve got mail!

And, to ALL of the women in my life and in my network, I am grateful to know you and to be learning from you. Cheers to climbing that U curve again, together.

14 years in this role today. That's hard to believe. Three things I am taking with me into the year ahead:

1️⃣ Leadership matters. 
I've learned that in schools and in organizations, leadership shapes everything. I've had the privilege of working alongside incredible educators across Chicago, and of being inspired by the way they distribute and develop leadership every day. I've also been honored to support and learn from the careers of many who started here at The Chicago Public Education Fund. They've gone on to teach, to lead their own organizations, and to champion the causes that matter most to them. Watching all of them shine is one of my purest joys.

2️⃣ Change is constant. Student experience has to be as well. 
I've watched as the demands on schools keep evolving. The set of stakeholders keeps shifting. Priorities, policies, and pressures get more complex. What I've learned to keep constant is our shared responsibility to ensure public schools help young people live into their best lives. Centering the experience of young people and their families helps keep learning the North Star.

3️⃣ When you know better, you have to do better. 
I've had 14 years of wins and made 14 years of mistakes. I've learned to apologize when I get it wrong and to ask for help. To give credit freely and whenever it is due. I've also learned that it doesn't really matter if it was a win or a loss, at least in the long run. What matters is that we use the experience to help improve personally, organizationally, and across the sector. I am excited about the years of learning ahead.

And one more thing: No matter the season or where I am, I have learned that starting my day with the sun and a walk makes me better at what I do (and maybe at who I am). My favorite work walk? Along the river to Lake Michigan and through my office door. (Photos courtesy of those AM walks.)

I’ll be taking the stage in an hour at the ASU+GSV Summit to talk about how school systems are approaching AI – and what it will take to get this right.

In recent conversations with school and system leaders, one tension keeps surfacing: how to balance protecting student data and maintaining trust, while also giving educators access to tools that can meaningfully reduce administrative burden.

District decisions: What tools are approved, how they’re implemented, and what guidance is provided – have real consequences for what school leaders and educators are able to do in practice.

We’re seeing this play out in Chicago, where strong, decentralized leadership is creating space for innovation, even in low-resource environments. 

But what’s also clear is that access alone isn’t enough. Without clear guidance and support, leaders are left to navigate these tools on their own. 

When they reach their limits, which almost all new tools do, that can mean the work shuts down.

The way this evolves will depend on the choices we make now.

The way it looks in 10 years depends entirely on what we decide to protect and what we design around.

Looking forward to learning alongside Mahnaz R. Charania, PhD, Jodi Feikema, PhD, Megan Mitchell, M.Ed, Jim O'Neill, and Jason Palmer, and continuing the conversation.

More to come. #ASUGSVSummit #EdTech #AIinEducation

There’s a lot of talk about federal funding in public schools—how it’s used, whether it’s effective, and if it’s necessary. But beyond the headlines and sound bites, I don’t see nearly enough discussion rooted in facts.

Here are three things you should know before weighing in on the future of federal education funding:

1️⃣ Federal funds were introduced to supplement state and local investments.
Title I, for example, was launched in 1965 when President Johnson declared “a national goal of Full Educational Opportunity,” charging the federal government with more actively supporting strong schools, especially in communities with limited financial wealth.

2️⃣ Even with federal support, the bulk of school funding comes from state and local sources.
In a district like Chicago Public Schools (CPS), where 72% of students are economically disadvantaged, federal funds make up approximately 16% (or $1.3 billion) of the district’s $8.4 billion operating budget. While essential, these funds supplement—not substitute—local investment.

3️⃣ Chicago’s principals have more flexibility than most in using these funds to meet student needs.
In many school districts, the use of federal dollars is decided centrally. But in CPS, principals work alongside Local School Councils to direct much of the funding where it will have the greatest local impact—whether through additional instructional staff, tutoring and after-school programs, mental health supports, or strategies to improve student attendance. This flexibility allows leaders to tailor resources to the specific needs of their school communities.

Over the next few weeks, I will highlight how different principals use federal funds to drive real student outcomes. I hope these examples will ground the debate in facts—because the future of our schools and the students they serve deserve nothing less.

Principal Barton Dassinger's recent Chicago Tribune op-ed (linked in the comments) tells a powerful story about what’s possible when school leaders have the flexibility and data to innovate with care for students and families.

At Cesar E. Chávez Elementary, Barton and his team increased attendance to 96% by focusing on daily practice rather than distant metrics. Through real-time data and daily adult routines, the Chávez team responds immediately when students are absent — calling families, problem-solving barriers, and, if needed, literally showing up at doors to walk students to school.

What stands out most is how the team’s approach and routines serve relationships. Data is used as a tool for connection and trust, helping Chávez evolve into one of Illinois’ top-performing neighborhood elementary schools.

Barton also emphasizes the importance of trusting principals to work with their communities, noting that his role as an Independent School Principal has given him the autonomy to design staffing, schedules, and support that truly meet his community’s needs. 

A powerful reminder that solutions to even pressing challenges, such as chronic absenteeism, exist — if we trust educators and families to pursue them.

This is what strong, equity-driven school leadership looks like: showing up every day, utilizing data effectively, and building systems rooted in trust. 

Congratulations to Barton and the Chávez community for modeling what’s possible for schools across Chicago.

This week, Principal Barton Dassinger of César E. Chávez Elementary School in Back of the Yards testified before the Illinois State Board of Education, and the most important part of his message wasn't about attendance itself. It was a direct ask: use the state's accountability system to flag student needs earlier, and resource schools to do the work that his community already does every day.

Under the current proposed framework, a student can be counted as having "consistent attendance" even if they miss more than three weeks of school. Barton asked ISBE to consider whether that threshold actually reflects what research tells us — or what educators see. It doesn't. Missing just five days is associated with lower grades and test scores. Students who miss a week of ninth grade are far less likely to graduate. The warning signs appear long before a child becomes “chronically absent.”

Barton isn't asking to rewrite the federal definition of chronic absenteeism. He's asking Illinois to use the flexibility it has to surface those signals sooner — and to back that up with real support for schools.

What does that support look like in practice? At Chávez, it starts every morning. Staff review who's missing and immediately begin reaching out — calls home, walking students to school, helping families solve transportation or childcare problems on the spot. In a community where economic hardship is common and where immigration enforcement has created genuine fear, showing up consistently depends on trust. Families have to believe the school is on their side. When they do, students come.

That's the model Barton is pointing to. Not just a better metric — but the infrastructure and relationships behind it.

Strong accountability systems work when they align what we know drives student success with the resources schools need. Barton's testimony made that case powerfully.|

Grateful for principals like Barton who show up for their communities and who use their voice to strengthen the systems that support schools across Illinois.

#ReturntoWork is a little anxiety-inducing. Do people still need me? Does anyone even remember me? How do I know? Am I going to be too tired by Thursday to think?

A few years ago, we introduced two tools at The Fund to help ease those feelings and to help the team embrace a returning colleague. 

This week, I experienced first-hand the beauty of: 

🎯 A “Need to Know” summary: This is a document and email that includes the returning team member’s major work streams, with a reminder of where things stood at the start of the leave, an update on their current status and coming deadlines, and key links. It is usually accompanied by an email that summarizes the most pressing items and highlights schedule/calendar items for the first few weeks back.

📅 A “soft return” week: This is an approach to return that intentionally centers the people/connection part of the work and that also aims to position the returning team member in a way that they can add immediate value. This week included a Board committee meeting, some site visits with principals, and several one-on-ones, all structured for reconnecting and dot-connecting (my personal superpower).

In addition, we engage in a “small comforts” approach to the return. This looks like a “Welcome Back” note in your space, flowers on your first day, donuts on Friday, and other small signals of care.

It is always a joy when something you theoretically believe in becomes something you KNOW works because it has a positive impact on YOU.

We’ve learned a lot over the past 25 years, but one truth remains: students don’t learn because of policy or politics. They learn — and thrive — when supported by excellent educators, surrounded by principled partners, and supplied with the essentials they deserve.

Lately, there’s been a lot of discussion around whether the Chicago Board of Education should approve a $175 million payment to reimburse the City for a pension payment to the Municipal Employees’ Annuity and Benefit Fund (MEABF). This will be the topic of two public hearings on the budget this week, March 13 and 14 at 10:30 a.m. at CPS’ Loop offices.

Simply put: CPS’s 2025 budget doesn’t have enough revenue to cover this payment AND meet the costs of a new teacher contract.

Amid the debate, let’s ground ourselves in some key facts about how CPS funds are allocated and what’s at stake if budgets tighten further.

📊 CPS’s $8.4B Operating Budget: Where Does the Money Come From?
58% from local sources ($5.0B, primarily property taxes)
25% from the state ($2.1B)
16% from federal funding ($1.3B, in Title resources, nutrition programs, and other grants)*

*Federal funding is declining.* 

Between FY24 and FY25, CPS lost $337M in federal funds as COVID-19 relief money dried up. The final $233M had to be spent by September 2024. 

And, as I have discussed before, there is talk about federal changes that might put Title I and other federal funding streams at risk.

💰 TLDR; we have about $8.4B, but are losing some revenue due to federal shifts. 

Got it. So, where does the money go right now?

$3.4B supports system-wide costs:
▪️ 56% ($1.9B) covers centrally managed resources like facilities, transportation, clinicians, social workers ($5800/student)
▪️ 37% ($1.3B) goes to teacher pensions and set-asides ($3,000/student).
▪️ 7% ($200M)  funds central administration like finance, IT, and legal etc. ($676/student).

$5B goes directly to schools (~$15,000 per student). Of that, up to 95% covers staff salaries.
▪️ Every school has a principal and at least one assistant principal (~$368K per school on average).
▪️ Schools have at least 10 teachers, with an average of 41 per school (~$5M per school on average).
▪️ Special education support is significant, with an average of 14 Special Education Classroom Assistants per school (~$1M per school on average).

This school year, CPS school communities budgeted about $100M in non-personnel funding (~$500/student), allocated at the discretion of principals and Local School Councils. 

This funding ($200K/school) supports:
✅ After-school programs & tutoring
✅ Athletics & extracurriculars
✅ Community school efforts, which keep buildings open 6 AM - 6 PM

What’s the Bottom Line?? 
🔽 
When schools in Chicago face funding gaps, principals don’t have the luxury of cutting nice-to-haves. They are often forced to cut what others would consider basics: sports teams, tutoring, and afterschool programming. The district has to cut shared supports - including those to students who need it most. 

The teachers who remain inevitably take on more inside their classrooms.

We must ask: As CPS navigates these challenges, how do we ensure that school leaders can provide the resources students and educators deserve?

“Tell me something GOOD about Chicago Public Schools.” I often hear this on soccer sidelines, at networking events, and in funder meetings. While some people pose it as a challenge, it is a joyful question for me, and I always have an answer.

It is an International Baccalaureate (IB) school, which means students learn a world language (Mandarin and Spanish), solve problems in their local communities, and connect with other students across the globe. When you walk in the door, their trophy case is full of artwork from pen pals who live thousands of miles away.

Kershaw is home to three cluster classrooms with students who have specialized needs, and the school has seen an influx of newcomers. In some places, people perceive these factors as a "burden" or "something to manage."

Kershaw recognizes every young person as the gift they are. They recite their student pledge every morning, which says: “I am the greatest child in the world simply because I am.” The adults in the building embody this belief through their welcoming, attentive, and supportive interactions with young people.

That belief makes a difference. Kershaw’s students outperform the state average in ELA and Mathematics growth, which means they learn more each year than their peers in other places.

The best part about this answer to the 'what's good' question in Chicago is that Kershaw isn't an individual outlier. At dozens of Chicago schools, adults consistently prioritize the needs of kids and families, making tough work look effortless. 

Doubt it? Come walk a school with me. I promise you’ll be glad you did!

What happens to schools if CPS has to cut their budgets beyond current levels?

Yesterday, I shared how a deficit greater than $229M could lead to reductions in school budgets. Today, I want to show what that could mean for individual schools.

In general, cuts would impact foundational staffing and discretionary spending levels, which will mean less academic, social, and emotional support for students citywide.

🔍 First, a reminder:
Current school budgets are flat compared to last year — but they assume CPS will secure $300M in new revenue. If that revenue doesn’t come through, the deficit could swell to $529M and could go higher still. That would mean almost all school communities would face real cuts.

📉 What could that look like?
Foundational Staffing: A typical large preK-8 school in Chicago has 1,000 students and 47 teacher positions. That’s one core teacher for every 26 students (39 teachers) and one holistic teacher for every five core teachers (8 teachers). A seemingly modest reduction in the core student-teacher ratio — say, from 26:1 to 27:1 — would mean cutting two core teachers and one holistic teacher. This could have a material and negative impact on student experience and could limit learning opportunities.

Flexible Funding: A typical small preK-8 school has about 300 students and receives around $200K in flexible funds. That’s enough to cover an additional teacher position and additional after-school programming, and allow for teachers to meet and plan outside of regular hours. A reduction by one-third — to $134K — is barely enough to cover that teacher position, and it would mean no planning time or after-school supports. A two-thirds reduction? It’s not enough to cover almost any staff position.

📊 This would play out in every school, adding up to:
$529M deficit = 1,500+ potential teacher layoffs
$700M deficit = 2,500+ potential teacher layoffs

The CPS budget is complex, from MEABF to TIFs to funding formulas, but the impact on kids is clear. We need to work now to make sure principals and LSCs aren’t forced to eliminate essential instructional and experiential supports for their students.

Let’s be honest about the impact of additional budget cuts, and just as clear about what’s at stake.

A few weeks ago, I wrote about Title I, one of the federal education programs reduced to sound bites in the media right now. 

Let’s take a step back.

In 1965, our country made a national commitment: A child’s zip code should not determine their destiny. Title I was created to ensure that talent and potential—no matter where they exist—are met with opportunity. 

Here’s the reality: Even in strong schools, students from communities with less inherited wealth face additional hurdles. If we truly believe in competition, innovation, and American excellence, we can’t afford to overlook that.

Look at George Westinghouse College Prep in Chicago’s East Garfield Park. It’s a high-performing, selective-enrollment high school with 80% of students taking advanced coursework—compared to about 25% statewide. 

That stat alone is impressive. But here’s what might surprise you: 73% of Westinghouse students come from low-income backgrounds, according to the state’s report card.

That percentage qualifies the school for about $3,000 per student in federal funds—resources that allow students at Westinghouse to access the same tools their suburban peers often take for granted. With that investment, the school can provide:
📌 Technology & instructional resources—ensuring students work with the digital tools required to compete in today’s economy.
📌 Daily access to iPads, Chromebooks, and charging carts— a necessity for interactive learning.
📌 STEM & career partnerships—connecting students to fields like healthcare, architecture, and engineering, preparing them for high-value careers.
Without this funding, experiences that fuel innovation and upward mobility—like advanced coursework and hands-on technology—would be out of reach. 

That’s not just unfair; it’s shortsighted.

The next time you hear someone question federal education funding, ask them this: Is $3,000 per student at Westinghouse wasteful? Or is it an investment in the skilled, competitive workforce we all need for the future?

When we invest wisely in education, we’re not just supporting students—we’re securing a future where we can all thrive.

October 10th is World Mental Health Day, and this year’s theme is Mental Health at Work. 

In the modern world, work is more of a state of being than a place. It can happen in an office, at your dining room table, on a phone, or in transit. In that context, a sizable majority of our waking hours are "at work."

For me, work is often the state I seek when I want to relieve stress. It is where I feel productively challenged, connected to my purpose, and in community, even across lines of difference. 

As a college student and young professional, if I felt confused about the social context or uncertain about a relationship, my default was to say that I had work to do and bury myself in a stack of books or edits. I often covered up social anxiety with academic ambition and buried hurt feelings with hard work.

As a young mom, if I was bored with the toddler games, I dug in on a project instead of figuring out a different way to connect. Lack of control or interest in one area materialized as a pursuit of complete competence in another. 

The rewards and celebrations often praised the workaholic pattern, which felt good.

In later years, work was more frequently a source of stress and burnout rather than solace. However, the long-term lack of full attention to other areas of my life left me feeling like work was the only thing I could do well.

It took me a lot of years (and therapy bills) to learn that I was using work to avoid more uncomfortable feelings of failure, uncertainty, and disconnection. I needed to do the work to find my purpose outside of the scope of The Fund's work. For me, that was and is still- hard work. 

It took me a long time to realize that what I like to do at work—dream, build, do—could translate to what I like to do as a mom. It took me a lot of trial and error to negotiate those dreams, creations, and actions around the evolving needs of four growing kids. When I get it right, I feel the same sense of accomplishment when I complete a strong funder ask or launch a new program.

It took me a lot of quiet and sometimes doing nothing to remember what I liked to read and how I liked to write. It took me even longer to find people who would hold me accountable for doing those things regularly. Now, when I read something I love or write something I don’t hate, it feels important to share it, almost as a promise to my future self.

It took scheduling meditation, therapy, church, and workouts and holding those times on my calendar in the same way I hold check-ins and financial reviews. Now, they are a part of my routine and serve as a buffer against the stressors that are inevitable in the world in which we live.
 
On this important day, I encourage you to consider where you feel healthiest and where you might need to pay more attention. It has certainly helped me.

In my work with the Illinois Literacy Foundation, I’ve learned that more than half of Illinois adults read and write English below a sixth-grade proficiency level. In practical terms, this makes work, family life, and civic participation more challenging for millions of people.

That reality shapes how I think about the public value of education—here in Chicago and nationwide. Literacy is foundational.

📖 Learning to read, and then reading to learn, underpins the critical thinking and decision-making adults need at home, at work, and in civic life. As technology and AI continue to accelerate, the urgency of this work only grows.

✅ The good news: progress is possible. School communities that advance literacy faster than average offer important insight into what it takes to secure these foundational skills for all students.

A recent piece by Chad Aldeman in The 74 (link in comments) provides an interactive map and highlights school communities nationwide that are outperforming expectations in early literacy. The study identifies 2,158 “exceptional” schools where third-grade reading scores are significantly higher than predicted. CPS has 22 public schools on that list.

🏫 One example is Goudy Technology Academy in Uptown. Goudy serves 490 students and is one of Chicago’s most diverse schools:

🌍 Nearly 50% of students are English learners
🤝 Roughly a third identify as Asian, a third as Black, and a third as Latino
📊 82% of students are identified as low-income on the state report card

Based on its student population, The 74 estimates Goudy’s expected reading proficiency rate at 16%.

▶️The actual rate is 39%—and rising, well above state and national averages of about 30%.

Understanding how that happens matters. At Goudy, Principal Bill Yeh and his team demonstrate what a sustained, schoolwide commitment to literacy looks like:
✅ A culture of data-informed instruction
✅ Consistent use of technology to support and differentiate learning
✅ Regular progress monitoring to meet individual student needs
✅ Timely resources and skill-building supports

▶️ The result: consistent, strong reading growth for low-income students.
Goudy is a powerful example of how a coherent curriculum, strong teacher collaboration, and a belief that all students deserve to read can improve outcomes.

And Goudy is not alone. Leaders like Tonya Williams-Weatherly (Ruggles), Barton Dassinger (Chavez), John Fitzpatrick (Locke), and Shelley Lugo Cordova (Greene) continue to show what’s possible when schools build strong instructional ecosystems, invest in teachers, and align supports around student needs.

Their success should inspire—and challenge—all of us.

With focused leadership and sustained commitment, many more CPS students can achieve grade-level reading proficiency. We must continue to learn from these bright spots and work to make results like Goudy’s the norm, not the exception.

Our students deserve nothing less.

“Losing isn’t very fun.” – My kid

My kids are not the kind who get excited about participation trophies. They like to win. And they have reached the point in their sports experiences where that isn’t always a given.

The “unfun” feeling of loss is one reason I’ve always struggled with trying to make failure “safe.” For me, there is nothing safe about the feeling of trying my best and coming up short.

I have learned a lot from watching my kids navigate in three dimensions this summer, though — they see winning, losing, and learning in ways I often miss.

It’s been interesting to watch their growth at a time when I am growing, too. In education, we often discuss #ProductiveStruggle. This summer, I have seen how good coaching manifests that concept beyond the classroom. 
I am reading #TheFrictionProject, which has helped me start to see some differences between their approach and mine.

First, my kids don't turn away from that friction when they don’t know how to do something or can’t reliably do it well. They lean into it and keep asking questions until they understand what is working or identify what might work better. It’s not just that they don’t give up.; they focus on improving in specific ways.

When I return to work, I want to foster more “learn-it-all” behavior in individuals and across teams. To start, I am thinking a lot about how check-in structures and mentorship might encourage specific continuous improvement.

Second, I have noticed that my kids’ best coaches — the ones who seem to get the best results — tell them what to “stop” doing as often as they tell them what to start. This ability to simplify rather than complicate a challenge is also an essential source of reflection.

The book suggests that leaders do more to remove friction around the “right” actions, and it’s been interesting to watch that in action. As I dive back into the day-to-day, I want to challenge myself to subtract more often than I add.

My kids seem to enjoy the process, even when it is most difficult. They take genuine pleasure in doing something they enjoy with people they like. They aim to be the kind of teammate whose positive energy is contagious. They accept friction as part of growth and try to make it worth it, even when it isn’t fun. 

The book says “friction fixers” help their colleagues do their best work, sometimes just reframing the group's experience. 

I’ve observed which kids (my own and others) play that role on a team. When I head back to work, I want to pay more attention to rewarding and valuing that contagious behavior, especially when tensions are high.

🔃 Last week, Chicago Public Schools (CPS) Interim CEO Dr. Macquline S King, EdD outlined a projected $734M gap between the district’s anticipated obligations and committed revenue.

What’s included in this number?
➖The $229M previously identified as the gap. 
➖$300M to account for the gap widening if expected revenue doesn’t materialize.
➕ $175M to reimburse the City of Chicago for costs related to pension expenses for non-teaching staff.
➕$30M for costs related to the transition of ACERO schools.

One option to narrow the gap without further negative impact on the student experience? 

💳Borrowing. 💳

CPS issues debt and uses other financial instruments to support capital needs, like constructing and maintaining schools. Borrowing also helps manage cash flow and liquidity needs.

Of course, debt has to be repaid. Borrowing today means revenue has to be diverted from teachers, programs, and services for many years in the future. 

That might be worth it to build or repair a building we will use for decades. It’s harder to make the case when borrowing pays for day-to-day costs like transportation or student supplies.

🛑Consider this: In FY25, CPS had total revenue of $9.34M. Of that, $800M was unavailable to meet today’s student needs. 
 
Why? It was paying interest on $9B in long-term debt that CPS holds. 

Some borrowing is inevitable in a district as large as Chicago. 

Long-term debt makes long-term capital improvements possible. But this isn’t about paying for buildings that will be here in 80 years - it’s paying for day-to-day operations.

And our debt load is already relatively high. CPS’s debt service cost is about 9% of total revenue. In recent years, it’s been as high as 10 to 15%. New York? 5% Los Angeles? 7%

Later this week, I’ll talk a little about CPS’s previous experience with borrowing to pay for operating expenses and about what that might look like this year.

FY27 Cost Explainer #1: Staffing costs

Salaries and benefits for 45,578 employees account for about $6.1B (~68%) of all CPS operating costs. On average, staffing costs grew 11% each year between FY19 and FY26 — while average revenue only increased by 6%.

When costs outpace new revenue, it forces tough choices for everyone.

Let’s break that down. 🔽 🔽

📣Headline: Most of CPS’ 45,000+ team members provide direct services to children and families.

37,427 (82%) of these people serve in schools. This includes:

✅ 22,468 teachers (49%) | Average salary: $100K 
      >>> Average annual salary increase since FY19: 4.2%

✅ 1,166 principals and assistant principals (3%)
522 Principals | Average salary: $176K 
      >>> Average annual salary increase since FY19: 3.0%
644 Assistant Principals | Average salary: $143K 
      >>> Average annual salary increase since FY19: 3.8%

✅ 13,793 (30%) support staff assigned to a school
For example: counselors, classroom assistants, school clerks
◼ Average salary varies by position, but overall: $57K   
      >>> Average annual salary increase since FY19: 4.7%

The remaining 8,151 include: 

✅ 6,432 (14%) citywide support staff budgeted centrally but working at schools 
For example: maintenance, transportation, and food service
◼ Average salary varies by position, but overall: $64K

Last week, our chief public affairs officer, Nelson Gerew, was invited to testify at the Illinois House Executive Committee subject-matter hearing on the Chicago Public Schools (CPS) budget. During his testimony, Nelson provided a historical overview of the district's finances from 2008 to 2025. Understanding this history is essential for establishing a solid financial foundation for the district's future.

Today's budget update: Liquidation as a tool 

CPS allocates positions to each school using a formula. It includes teachers, assistant principals, restorative justice coordinators, and other roles.

Those positions may not match what the school needs or who the principal has on staff. When a mismatch occurs, the principal can work with the Local School Council (LSC) and the district to liquidate the position. This converts dollars tied to that position to more flexible funding. 

That flexibility allows principals and their school communities to hire for other positions, purchase materials, or fund external programs in alignment with their specific needs.

The problem in FY27 is that schools receive fewer dollars per liquidated role.
In FY26, liquidating a position returned 91-97% of its average cost. In FY27, that drops to 50-58%.

→ What does this mean for a school?

A school that liquidated two teachers and a restorative justice coordinator in FY26 received $341,000. The same decisions in FY27 would result in $141,000 less. That gap is an entire teaching position.

→ How widespread is this challenge?

In FY26, 96 (19%) schools liquidated 130 positions, freeing up $11.9M. The same decisions in FY27 would free up $5.7M (52% less).

→ What are the benefits of this change?

For schools, there is no upside. 

For the district, the gap between FY26 and FY27 is a potential savings. Final numbers won't be clear until June, but if patterns hold, the maximum benefit to the district is $6M, on top of the $96M saved through school cuts.

Of course, with less to gain, fewer principals may liquidate roles. They may choose to keep positions that don’t quite fit their vision and forgo the supplies, programs, and support that flexible dollars used to fund.

→ The bottom line

The maximum district savings here is 0.8% of the $732M deficit.

A small gain for the system. A real loss of flexibility for principals and the communities they serve.

At the end of December, two important decisions were made, both of which impact Chicago Public Schools and its FY26 budget.

First, the City of Chicago adopted its 2026 budget, which includes a record $1.01 billion Tax Increment Financing (TIF) surplus that must be distributed to local taxing bodies. Under that plan, CPS will receive approximately $552.4 million—about $193 million more than originally budgeted for in CPS’s FY26 forecast.

Of that amount, approximately $175 million will be reimbursed to the City for a portion of the Municipal Employees’ Annuity and Benefit Fund (MEABF) pension costs associated with CPS non-teaching staff. 

The confirmed surplus helps CPS maintain stability in a year that began with a projected $734 million deficit. But as always, TIF revenue is one-time and unpredictable. And with the City signaling a move away from TIFs, CPS will need more reliable, long-term funding solutions in the years ahead.

Second, the Chicago Board of Education voted 15–5 to pass a resolution allowing Chicago Public Schools to pursue up to $41M in additional property tax revenue.

This option is available because property values grew faster than expected, and the revenue would support CPS’s operating budget, pension obligations, and special education transportation.

What stood out in the December CBOE meeting was the quality of the discussion. Board members grappled openly with two competing imperatives: managing costs responsibly and ensuring schools are fully funded. Those goals are aligned in theory, but deeply challenging to balance in practice, given the district’s financial reality.

In the end, the Board voted in favor of the increase, while offering substantial material for continued discussion and debate about long-term revenue options and structural cost savings. These conversations will overlap with TIF discussions at the City and with ongoing state-level debates.

Actively grappling with these questions and tensions is a healthy sign—especially given that initial decisions on the FY27 CPS budget, where the gap may be as much as $500 million, need to be made soon.

More to come as that planning gets underway.

I have been reading a lot (and writing a little) about the budget decisions facing the Chicago Board of Education and the CPS leadership team. Their choices will impact students, teachers, principals, and communities today and in the future. This piece is an essential read for those trying to understand the stakes.

Today the Chicago Board of Education will hold a special meeting to consider whether to pursue additional revenue related to property taxes.

A few basics, in plain terms:

Why is $41M “available” now?
Earlier this year, CPS set its property tax levy below the maximum allowed under state law. 

The final 2024 Estimated Assessed Value for the City of Chicago had not yet been published, and the amount of new property in Chicago was higher than expected. 

As a result, the district now has the legal option, not the obligation, to levy up to $41 million more than originally planned. 

Of this $41M:
- Around $24M would be part of the education levy, to support the district’s overall operating budget;
- Around $11M would go to the district’s pension levy, to pay costs related to the Chicago Teacher’s Pension Fund; and
- Around $6M would go to cover costs related to special education transportation.

What choices does the Board have? 

At least two:
1️⃣Leave the levy as-is and not pursue the additional $41M
2️⃣Approve some or all of the $41M in additional property tax revenue

In any case, the FY26 levy must be finalized by December 29.

None of these choices is simple, and each carries real implications for taxpayers, schools, and long-term stability.

Why does this matter in the bigger picture?

CPS is facing an operating deficit of over $500 million in FY27. In that context, $41M is not a solution—but it is also not insignificant. It represents about 8% of the projected gap, and is the equivalent of ~360 teaching positions. 

Decisions like this signal how the district and Board are thinking about closing a much larger structural shortfall; signals the city and state will be monitoring closely.

This meeting is less about one revenue line and more about how CPS navigates hard fiscal realities: balancing stability for schools, transparency for taxpayers, and the urgency of long-term planning.

Chicago’s students, educators, and communities deserve clear-eyed conversations about tradeoffs—especially when the numbers are this large and the stakes this high.

FY27 Revenue Explainer #1: Federal Funding 
It's budget season in CPS, and this space will be full of fiscal news you can use.

Starting this week: the revenue side of the equation. Most school systems draw from three sources: federal, state, and local. We'll take them one at a time. 

Up first: federal funding.

Federal dollars have never been the primary driver of school funding in the U.S. But for specific students and programs, they are essential.

CPS can expect roughly $900M in federal support in FY27, largely flat from the prior year, and about 9% of an estimated $10.25B total budget.

The largest federal streams for CPS in FY27 are:
◾ $487M: Every Student Succeeds Act (ESSA); also known as “title dollars,” this revenue is designed to supplement local and state funding for districts serving low-income families
◾ $214M: Child nutrition programs
◾ $115M: IDEA: services for students with disabilities

Congress recently extended level funding across these programs. 

These dollars are more stable than headlines suggest, but not immune to fluctuations that impact schools and young people.

Smaller, discretionary grants within the larger allocations are more exposed. Last year, CPS lost a $23M magnet school grant with little warning. Those kinds of changes can happen mid-year, without replacement.

BOTTOM LINE: For CPS and other systems nationwide, federal contributions are likely to remain flat, with some exposure to sudden shifts around the edges. In SY27, the federal contribution won’t meaningfully close structural gaps, and small mid-year shifts could have an outsized impact. 

📌 Next: state funding – the most important lever for long-term stability.

Earlier this week, I shared updates about the $529 million budget gap facing Chicago Public Schools in 2026. 

There’s no easy fix—but one potential source of revenue worth discussing is Tax Increment Financing (TIF). Let’s explore what that means.

🙋 What is a TIF?
It’s a tool a city can use when it decides to invest in development in a particular community. To do so, it freezes property tax revenue for schools and other local bodies at the current rate. As the neighborhood grows and tax revenue increases, the extra money is banked to fund payments for the original development and help build new amenities, such as roads or parks, within the same neighborhood. 

⁉️How does TIF work in Chicago?
Chicago has been using TIFs since 1983 and has 136 of these areas, according to the latest count. TIFs are intended to remain active for 23 years, at which point the increased revenue would benefit the entire city and other taxing bodies, such as CPS, not just the TIF community. These can be extended for an additional 12 years, with state approval. Approval was secured for eight TIF districts in December 2024; the city plans to seek approval to extend another ten through 2027.

🏫 How does this affect schools in CPS?
Schools do not benefit from increased tax revenue while the TIF is active. In 2025, over $1.2 billion in taxes were allocated to TIF funds. CPS says this means it is missing out on about $600 million each year that could be used to support students and teachers.

💲 What’s a TIF surplus?
 If a TIF area has money left over that isn’t being used for a project, the city is supposed to share that money with groups that usually get property taxes, including CPS. Since schools typically receive about half of all property taxes in Chicago, CPS gets approximately 50% of any TIF surplus.

In fiscal year 2025, CPS received $298 million from surplus TIF funds. That’s a big jump from $159 million in fiscal year 2024, but there’s more money being held in TIFs that could help.

🛠️ What could be done?
Options include: 
1️⃣ Declaring more TIF money as surplus; CPS receives about 50%.
2️⃣ Shrink some TIF areas to let more money go back to schools and other agencies.
3️⃣ End certain TIFs, ensuring CPS and other services fully benefit from the existing tax base.

TIFs are tricky. And, if we’re serious about ensuring CPS has the resources it needs to serve the city’s students, it is essential to understand and consider the role they could play.

Last Friday, the Chicago Board of Education (CBOE) approved the FY2026 budget—totaling $10.25B.

As required by state law, the budget’s assumed revenues match its projected costs. Including:
$1.1B in debt service
$556M in capital spending
$8.6B in operating expenditures

The $8.6B operating budget is a 1% increase over FY2025, and required difficult but necessary cuts as federal COVID-19 funding phased out. 

When she began her tenure in June of 2025, Macquline S King, EdD  projected the district’s structural deficit was $734M, inclusive of the district reimbursing the city of Chicago $175M for a portion of the MEABF pension payment.

Thanks to the leadership of Dr. King, input from five community feedback sessions, and the decisions reflected in the new budget, those projections have been dramatically reduced—by nearly 40%. Two big shifts:

While the MEABF reimbursement is likely to remain a topic of discussion, there is general consensus that it should not be included as a budgeted obligation, without corresponding revenue. This removes $175M from the structural deficit assumptions.

The approved FY26 budget permanently eliminated $214M in central office services and through operational efficiencies.

This means real decreases in deficit projections for future years:

FY2027: $520M (↓47%)
FY2028: $582M (↓44%)
FY2029: $835M (↓37%)

Of course, with a $500M+ gap still forecast for FY27, the road ahead won’t be easy. Future cuts will be harder to find, and true long-term stability will require partnership among Chicago Public Schools leadership, the CBOE, the city of Chicago, and the state of Illinois—to pursue both new revenue sources and efficiencies, while avoiding further borrowing.

The FY26 budget is complete. Next up: FY2027. I’ll share updates in the weeks and months ahead as that process begins.

Earlier this week, I shared that Chicago Public Schools (CPS) now spends $800M annually on debt—funds that could otherwise support classrooms, teachers, and student services.

🏫Not all debt is bad. Borrowing for long-term capital projects, like modernizing aging school buildings, is standard in large districts. 

But borrowing to plug year-to-year budget gaps? That’s a different story.

Unfortunately, it’s one we’ve heard before. 

In 2016, CPS issued $725M in debt at 8.5% interest to close a deficit.
💲That deal alone costs $62M/year in interest through 2044.

Between 2016-2018, CPS issued over $2.1B in similar deals.
💲Freeing up short-term cash but ultimately locking in nearly $200M/year in interest payments.

Thankfully, in 2017, Illinois passed a new education funding model that improved the district's financial outlook. But the debt the district took on to bridge the gap, and its long-term consequences, remain.

After all, if CPS had that $200M back today, the current budget situation would be less worrisome.

❓Are there new revenue solutions on the horizon? ❓

Maybe, but they will take leadership.

There’s been understandable confusion about how the City’s budget negotiations might affect CPS. Here are the key facts.

💡 Let’s start with the CPS context.

- CPS built $379M in TIF surplus into its FY26 budget, approved in August. Schools used this number for their own planning.
- The initial proposed City budget included $552.4M in TIF surplus for CPS, around 52% of the total $1B TIF surplus declared citywide. 
- The $173 million above what was included in CPS’ approved budget is committed to help the City meet its Municipal Employees’, Officers’, and Officials’ Annuity and Benefit Fund (MEABF) pension payment. This was solidified with an Intergovernmental Agreement approved by the CBOE on 10/30. 

🔍 What We Know About the TIF Surplus

- In October, the Mayor’s proposed budget included a record $1B TIF surplus.
- By law, $552.4M of that surplus flows to CPS. That’s its share of the property tax revenue designated for schools that is held in TIF districts.
- Even though the City Council’s Finance Committee rejected the Mayor’s initial budget revenue proposal in November, that vote does not necessarily affect the surplus. In fact, in other alternative plans that have been proposed, the city’s revenue plan still includes up to $1B in TIF surplus. 
- Unless the total TIF surplus in the final City budget falls below around $700M, CPS’ current-year budget remains intact.
- The Intergovernmental Agreement, between CPS and the City of Chicago, makes it clear that CPS is only obligated to make the MEABF payment if it receives above $379M in TIF surplus, and the amount it contributes will be equal to the additional amount it receives (but is not to exceed $200M).

🗓️ What Happens Next
- The City Council must pass a budget by December 31.
- The only scenario in which CPS’s portion is affected is if the total surplus falls below $700M. None of the current proposals suggests that as an option.
- For any decrease between $1B and $700M, CPS would owe a smaller (or no) MEABF reimbursement to the City under the recent Intergovernmental Agreement; however, the CPS operational budget would remain unchanged. 

🏫 Impact on Schools
- Assuming a budget is passed that includes at least $700M in TIF surplus, no mid-year cuts are expected.
- Additional TIF dollars (above $379M) would support a City pension obligation (MEABF)—not CPS operations.

📘 Looking Ahead to FY26
The confirmed surplus helps CPS maintain stability in a year that began with a projected $734M deficit. But as always, TIF revenue is one-time and unpredictable. And with the City signaling a move away from TIFs, CPS will need more reliable, long-term funding solutions in the years ahead.

🎯 Bottom Line
- CPS will likely receive sufficient TIF dollars to cover its operating budget.
- Any revenue beyond $379M is already allocated to help cover MEABF payments.
- Chicago still needs sustainable revenue solutions to support students and schools.

As Chicago Public Schools (CPS) prepares to pass and implement its FY26 budget, sources of additional revenue have been a major focal point over the past months. The most likely revenue source in this cycle? Surplus funds from the city’s Tax Increment Financing (TIF) districts.

💰 What’s a TIF surplus?
 Each year, the city of Chicago must declare unspent dollars from certain TIF districts as “surplus.” By state law, CPS is guaranteed about 52% of any declared surplus.

▶️CPS’s FY26 budget proposal includes $379M in TIF surplus from the city; flat from FY25.◀️

📈 What assumptions are built in here?

▪️That the city will declare a surplus of ~$700M. In that scenario, CPS would receive its share - ~$379M - and the city would receive ~$190M.
▪️Most experts anticipate the city will need to declare at least some surplus to close its own projected budget gap - estimated at $1.2B.
▪️There are funds available as surplus. As the visual shows, the last city of Chicago annual report indicated TIF balances over $3B and a $485M surplus net of all revenue, expenditure, declared surplus, and planned projects.

🔎Looking ahead
The city is exploring options to become less reliant on TIF surplus in the future, but major shifts are not likely before FY27. 

Whatever approach the city takes, CPS is entitled to the related property tax revenue. Long term, property tax revenue not placed in a TIF district account would go directly to CPS; this may be more predictable than the current approach.

Existing revenue increases related to property taxes may not be enough. Many stakeholders are already advocating for collaborative conversations among state, city, and CPS leadership as soon as this budget cycle concludes.

Bottom line: A TIF surplus is likely for FY26 and is vital to helping CPS balance its $734M budget deficit. However, it won’t solve CPS’s long-term structural deficit. Later this week, I will discuss how additional funding from the state can help on that front.

This week, Chicago Public Schools (CPS) hosted a learning session, and three community feedback sessions focused on the 2025-26 budget. The goal? To provide information and context about the current budget, and to hear directly from the public on possible solutions.

Let’s dive into some of the information and data discussed and review the next steps for the coming weeks.

School budgets for the 2025-26 school year were built around a $229M deficit and submitted in early June. Even in this relatively “flat” context, many schools had to make difficult tradeoffs. 

On June 28, CPS’ Interim CEO Dr. Macquline S King, EdD anchored the discussion on the gap between allocated revenue and projected expenses, which is $734M—$500M more than schools planned for.

CPS revenue options are indeed limited. Local sources account for 57% of revenue, and CPS is limited in how much it can extend its property tax levy.

They will also host another learning session during the week of July 21. Once the sessions are completed, CPS will incorporate the feedback they’ve heard and continue to work with key stakeholders to finalize and post the full district budget by August 13. Quick recap: Launched in the 1960s as a part of the nation’s shared commitment to strong public schools for all, Title I aims to help “level the playing field” in a system where local and state funding is often dependent on generational property wealth. Title I recognizes that potential is everywhere, but opportunity can be limited. It aims to unlock student learning everywhere.

At Sumner Elementary Math and Science Community Academy in West Garfield Park, students are growing in math proficiency faster than 60% of their peers statewide.

At Owens Community Academy in West Pullman, students are outpacing two-thirds of their statewide cohort in reading. 

At both schools, more than 85% of students come from low-income households.

Their academic progress is not accidental. 

It’s supported by strong leadership and critical federal funding. Federal sources provide more than $4500 per student in these schools, giving principals more flexibility to invest in what students need most: additional teachers, smaller class sizes, targeted supports, enrichment programming, and more.

But, Title I and federal funds cover only a small portion of what it takes to run a school. When they are threatened, so is the stability and momentum that make academic progress possible.

As CPS Chief Education Officer Bogdana Chkoumbova put it at the start of the 2024-25 school year:

“When given adequate resources, CPS showed that we will make wise investments that support teaching and learning... We must continue to work toward a future where public education is valued as the most foundational part of a thriving society.”

Title I was established to level the playing field. Today, it remains one of our most effective tools for doing so; just look to Sumner and Owens for proof.

But, changes to Title I, especially at a time when other funding is flux, could be devastating. We must maintain it, protect it, and ensure it remains flexible in the hands of school leaders who know their students best.

Today's budget update: AP positions in small schools

Schools with enrollments of 250 or fewer are less likely to lose teacher positions in FY27. But they are losing something else: an assistant principal.

→ How did we get here? 

Starting in FY25, CPS allocated a foundational AP position to every school. Schools could use the funds tied to that allocation in other ways, but most principals and their learning communities prioritized retaining the AP position. In FY26, 499 district-operated schools received an AP allocation. Only 12 (2%) chose to redirect those resources. Among the 107 schools with fewer than 250 students, just 6 (6%) redirected those funds.

→ What's changing? 

CPS will no longer fund a foundational AP for schools with 250 or fewer students in FY27. That means slightly over 100 AP positions are likely to be cut. The district saves around $18M, about 19% of school-level savings identified so far ($96M), and 2.5% of the total $732M deficit.

→ What does this mean for schools? 

Trade-offs. APs provide real value: instructional leadership, administrative capacity, community connection, and a potential successor when principals transition.

Principals can use discretionary funds to keep the position, but an AP averages $180,000 in salary and benefits. Among schools with fewer than 250 students in FY26, the average discretionary funding was around $260,000. Assuming that holds steady in FY27, keeping an AP will be difficult for most schools. Those dollars are already covering critical operational needs, including supplies and transportation for field trips. Using funds to keep the AP means real trade-offs.

→ Are there other options? 

Sort of. Next week, I'll talk about position liquidation, another budget option principals have, but one that may be less useful in FY27.

Last week, the Illinois State Board of Education (ISBE) released proposed updates to the system that keeps the public informed about all Illinois public schools.*

What Illinois is proposing:

ISBE wants to create a “profile of performance” for each school using two sets of indicators:

Core indicators, which are the primary drivers of a school’s rating:
- Academic proficiency: % of students meeting/exceeding standards on state assessments (IAR for elementary/middle school; ACT for high school)
- Academic growth: how much students improve over time on those assessments
- Graduation rate: for high schools only

Elevating indicators, which can raise a school’s rating, a level, but not lower it:
- English Learner progress: whether multilingual learners are on track to reach English proficiency within 5 years
- Consistent attendance: % of students attending at least 90% of school days
- School culture & climate: student response rate on the 5Essentials survey

Each indicator has thresholds that determine a rating: Exemplary, Approaching Exemplary, Commendable, Developing, or Comprehensive. Those ratings then combine into a school’s overall designation, ranging from Exemplary (the highest rating) to Comprehensive.

A couple of other features worth noting:
- This system isn’t based on a simple weighted formula; ratings are determined by a combination and interaction of results across Core and - ---Elevating indicators. While this may seem appropriately nuanced to expert users, it can lead to confusion, especially for non-educators, including parents, who hope to use the system. 
- On the equity front, some decidedly good news: outcomes for all student groups matter: a school cannot receive an Exemplary or Approaching Exemplary designation if one or more student groups have a Comprehensive performance profile.

What’s next:
ISBE expects to approve the final plan at its April board meeting and submit it to the U.S. Department of Education. If approved, the new designations would appear on the Illinois Report Card in October.

How to get involved:
ISBE is hosting virtual listening sessions in January, February, and March, with public comment opportunities in March and April. Details are available at the link in the comments.

Our own director of policy and public affairs, Barry Tyler Jr., testified before the Board on the proposal in December (linked in comments as well).
Illinois has an opportunity to continue leading the nation by getting this system right—and we’ll keep sharing updates as the process moves forward.

* As a reminder, all states are required by federal law to have an accountability system that measures factors like academic proficiency, academic growth, and graduation rates. ISBE’s proposal complies with this law.

Graduation Rates in Chicago: What the Data Show (And What They Don’t)

Over the past few weeks, I highlighted data that shows how young people in Chicago are doing in school. I discussed how elementary assessments suggest progress with significant room to grow, and how stubbornly high absenteeism impacts learning environments. 

Today, we are examining another key indicator in more detail: high school graduation rates.

The Big Picture
CPS rightfully touts the district’s increased graduation rates as one of its most impressive accomplishments in its modern era. As CPS moved to a decentralized model in the 1990s, the graduation rate rose steadily from the 40s to over 75% by 2013.

This upward trend has remained a bright spot for CPS, even during the challenging years of the COVID pandemic. While the district posted its highest-ever graduation rate (83.2%) in 2022, the rate has remained above 80% in each of the three years since, and this year increased by 1.6 percentage points to 82.5%.

Why This Matters
Gains in the four-year graduation rate show that high school students in Chicago and across Illinois are making academic progress. While these numbers don’t by themselves indicate how students will perform in postsecondary education, coinciding rises in high schoolers taking college-level coursework through International Baccalaureate, Advanced Placement (26.4% in 2024-25), and dual-credit classes (20.7% in 2024-25) do suggest that more students are leaving high school ready to further their education.

The Bottom Line
While many metrics indicate that there is still considerable room for improvement, CPS’s achievements in improving graduation rates have made a tangible difference. If this year’s cohort graduated at a rate comparable to just 12 years ago, nearly 2000 fewer students would have walked across the stage last spring to collect their diplomas. The impact of increased graduation rates on these students is incalculable.

✨ Chicago’s students are proving what’s possible in public education. The question is: can adults keep up?

From Farragut grads heading to Cornell, to Chávez seventh graders completing Algebra I, our young people are delivering results at scale. They deserve leaders who match their resolve with transparency, focus, and investments in strategies that drive their growth.

Over the past 30 years, Chicago Public Schools has come so far. That wasn’t an accident. It was the result of decades of work by principals, teachers, scholars, and families. Crucially, it was driven by honest analysis of student data, which guided principals to deliver targeted support and accelerate learning where it was needed most. If we want to accelerate improvements in student outcomes, we must trust and empower local leaders to do what they do best.

The fact is, our students continue to hold up their end of the bargain by showing up with energy and effort. In response, they aren’t asking for reinvention, but for consistent opportunity and access to the excellence they deserve. It’s time for the rest of us to deliver.

On Wednesday, Chicago Public Schools (CPS) released its FY26 proposed budget. In a world of tough decisions, CPS leadership avoided additional cuts to schools, protecting the budgets principals and LSCs approved in June.

💲 Revenue: The budget assumes $379M in Tax Increment Financing (TIF) surplus, equal to FY25. The city likely needs TIF surplus to balance its own budget, and CPS is entitled to 52% of any surplus declared. The budget also includes a level increase in state funding of $76M as CPS’ need status in Illinois increased from Tier 2 to Tier 1. Tier 1 districts statewide receive priority for equity-based funds. The budget also indicates CPS would reimburse the city for a portion of non-teacher pension costs if additional revenue, above the TIF and state funding assumed, is received.

🛑 Reductions and cuts: The budget includes $293M in cuts to central office departments and citywide services. $165M was identified in June, including changes in food service and delays to non-essential maintenance. Another $126M was announced on Wednesday. Overall, central office staff will decrease from 1,662 in FY25 to 1,509 in FY26, a 10% decrease. Beyond layoffs, these cuts include a freeze on hiring and a delay in planned IT projects. 

🏦 Borrowing: No loan provision is included in the budget, as revenue and expenses are balanced with the assumptions outlined above. In public polling and community conversations earlier this year, taking a loan was an unpopular option. For reference, the FY26 budget already includes $1B in debt service for long-term loans, and an additional $23M was for interest from short-term loans to manage cash flow.

1️⃣ Make further cuts: Dr. King has stated that additional cuts should not come from schools, which is consistent with the feedback received in community conversations. Long term, CPS’s community conversations highlighted the need for coordinated advocacy around revenue, with the goal of securing a lasting solution.

4️⃣ Reassess pension contributions: Although it contributed a portion of its COVID-19 funding toward the MEABF obligations for a few years, CPS is not legally required to provide the city with an MEABF reimbursement. With COVID-19 relief funding fully spent and additional federal cuts looming, the trade-offs here are especially challenging.

Chicago has 77 neighborhoods, but it runs on six degrees of separation. And while leaning on others for support and advancement isn't always our first instinct, those networks are both available and invaluable.

Those networks didn't emerge by accident. In 1989, Illinois passed legislation that established Local School Councils, giving parents and community members a voice in their schools. Among the most important powers afforded to LSCs then and now: the responsibility for hiring a principal.

Over time, that decision fundamentally changed who leads schools in Chicago. Today, schools are more frequently led by women and by principals who identify as Black or Latino.

Research and experience tell us that representation matters - students are more likely to succeed when taught or led by an educator who shares some aspect of their identity. We also know that shifts in representation can be bumpy, and that networks, allyship, and mentorship matter, especially when someone is serving as the "first" or the "only."

Over the past few weeks, our team has been talking with Black principals and their mentors about their experiences leading in our schools. What keeps coming up in those conversations is the power of Black mentorship, genuine relationships, and connections across Chicago's schools and through the generations.

Take the story of Herald Watson, for example. Herald was a fourth-grade teacher when Stephen McClain, Ed.D. became his principal at Curtis Elementary in 2013. One day, Stephan called Herald into his office for what Herald calls "a real, heart-to-heart talk." At that moment, he realized Stephen saw him — not just as a teacher, but as a future leader. That conversation changed everything.

In 2025, Herald was named the principal of Lavizzo Elementary in Roseland. The school serves 375 students, most of whom identify as Black (86%). His first focus is to make the school a place all of his students want to be. He shared, "We have empowered our students to be co-creators of their school experience. Through Student Town Halls, focus groups, and empathy surveys, we gain insight into how our school feels, looks, and sounds to our scholars."

In his first year in the role, Herald has significantly increased attendance: 40% of students maintain attendance above 95%, and 24% attend at 90% or above. In 2024-2025, the average daily attendance rate was 88%. This year, Herald expects it to be 92% or above, with momentum to reach 95% in the next two years.

Stephan didn’t stop with inspiring Herald and students like him to lead. Today, he's coaching five principals through our Malott Educator Fellowship, empowering them to live into their why and increasing students’ sense of belonging.

As Black History Month concludes, we recognize the Black leaders who built this relational infrastructure and who are nourishing it today.

That's the work. That's the legacy.

On June 5, CPS principals submitted their final school budgets — based on a projected $229M deficit. While the overall budgets were technically "flat," most schools experienced reductions that required tough decisions.

📍Take Walt Disney Magnet School in Uptown as an example: Disney serves 1,394 students and is among the most diverse in the city: 55% of its students are Black, 20% are Latino/a/x, 12% are white, and 9% are Asian. 63% are identified as “economically disadvantaged.”

In FY25:
	✅Disney received 64 core/holistic positions
	✅Disney received $1.2M in discretionary funds and hired 10 essential staff (e.g., clerks, TAs)

In FY26:  Disney faced some reductions, despite enrollment remaining steady.
	✅63 core/holistic positions (-1 FTE)
	✅$1.1M in discretionary funding (-$100,000)

As Principal Paul Riskus, EdD shared recently, his team turned to fundraising to close the gap. This is a heavy lift for an already busy Disney staff. It’s also a tool not available to every school.

Of course, the situation could get worse.
 	▪️Current budgets assume $300M in revenue from city/state sources.
	▪️If that money doesn’t materialize the deficit rises to $529M, triggering deeper cuts.

Here’s what that would mean for Disney:
🚫 Lose one-third of discretionary funding → $370K 
	 📉 That could lead to a loss of up to 3 positions

🚫 Increase student-teacher ratio by just 1 → Loss of three teachers 
	📉 That could mean two core and one holistic teachers

Combined, that’s a 7% staffing loss (excluding special education). And it would happen just before school starts.

So close to the beginning of the school year, Disney would turn to its internal accounts (funds built from efforts such as fundraising, rentals, etc.) to save these positions, a difficult decision considering so much of this fund has already been depleted in the past two years. This is not sustainable and is not an option for many CPS schools.

Citywide, CPS elementary schools could see:
📉 $53M less in discretionary = 420+ teacher positions lost
📉 313 fewer teachers due to formula changes

There’s no question the CPS budget is complicated, but we can all agree that we need to do everything possible to avoid further reducing already limited school resources.

Last week, CPS announced a $732M deficit for FY27, up from the $520M projected in the FY26 Budget Book.

School-level budgets absorb nearly $100M of that gap. How CPS closes the rest is still an open question.

→ The most concrete revenue lever right now is TIF surplus.

CPS is assuming $100M, about a fifth of last year's actual surplus. Assuming $552M, equal to last year, TIFs would close roughly $450M of the gap.

That is not a permanent fix. But for FY27, it matters.

→ As CPS works through the big-picture issues, principals are facing the first significant school-level cuts since FY17.

Two changes to note:
▸ The student-to-teacher ratio rose by one student across all schools. Final savings will be clear in June; initial estimates suggest $78M.
▸ Schools under 250 students will no longer be guaranteed an assistant principal. That affects 100 to 120 positions and yields an estimated savings of $18M.

CPS made important choices to protect the most vulnerable schools, especially caps on teacher losses per school and a firm commitment to fully fund special education staffing.

With those caps in place, an estimated 800 to 900 positions could be affected systemwide — roughly 2% of the 37,427 people who work directly in CPS schools.

A small percentage on a spreadsheet means real people in school buildings. For the communities absorbing the cuts, the impact is anything but marginal.

→ What's next
Principals have until June 9 to appeal allocations, work with their Local School Councils, and finalize budgets. The Fund is providing budget tools and direct support through this window.

The district has until August 29 to pass a budget for FY27. Closing a deficit this size for two years running is not a sustainable path. 

Alongside the immediate work on FY27, it's time to align on long-term solutions to the structural problem.

More to come.

What could Chicago schools face if the CPS deficit grows?

Over the past few weeks, I’ve shared that there are multiple scenarios for CPS’ FY26 budget, with a deficit that could range from $229M to over $1B. That range is driven by uncertain revenues and big-picture cost drivers. Where Chicago lands within that range has very real implications for school communities.

🧮 Here’s what we know:
Last week, principals and LSCs received school budgets based on a $229M deficit, the smallest scenario among three considered. CPS can close a $229M deficit with cuts to centrally-provided services and keep overall school budgets flat — at about $5B across all schools.

❗But overall flat funding doesn’t mean unchanged budgets.
CPS school funding formulas reflect both enrollment and student need, and these change from year to year. That means most schools will still face trade-offs, even under the most stable scenario. That’s why we’re working with our partners to support principals and LSCs now.

❓But what if the deficit is larger? $529M? $734M? More?
Then, district-wide school-level budget cuts are likely, and CPS could:

Alter the foundational position formulas: In FY25, over 13,000 teacher positions were allocated via these formulas. Reducing this total by 500 teacher positions — one per school on average — would save just ~$60M, while reducing student supports everywhere.

Cut flexible funding: In FY25, preK-8 schools received an average of $650 per student, and at least $325 per student in flexible funding. High schools received an average of $1,500, and at least $1,095 per student. School communities use these resources for additional positions, supplies, programming, and meeting other student needs. Reducing this amount by a third — an average loss of $132K per school — would save only around $80M, and would require real reductions in the services offered to students in schools.

💡 Taking these tough steps would only yield ~$140M in savings on top of the central cuts of $239M. The cuts required to close a $529M deficit would likely be double what is described above in most schools. And, the larger the deficit, the more drastic these kinds of cuts will need to be.

School leaders are already working hard to meet student needs under the current conditions. If revenue assumptions don’t hold, they may be asked to do much more with even less. I’ll share more on what those difficult choices could look like tomorrow.

Budget topic of the day: Teacher allocations

CPS allocates core teaching positions to schools based on two factors: enrollment and a student-to-teacher ratio. For schools with more than 250 students, this can lead to compounding losses in FY27.

Enrollment declined by about 9,000 in FY26. That loss was experienced unevenly, with some communities losing larger numbers than others.

Simultaneously, CPS increased the student-to-teacher ratio by one student across all schools and grade bands. For many schools districtwide, this meant additional position losses. 

Most schools below 250 students in enrollment will not lose any teacher positions. Of the 107 schools in this category, 16 (15%) are expected to lose a teacher position. 

The 392 schools with more than 250 students are impacted by both enrollment changes and an increase in the student-to-teacher ratio by one student across all schools and grade bands. 

369 (94%) of these schools are expected to lose at least one teacher position as a result of the shifts.  

While the final impact won’t be clear until June, this likely means the loss of 700-800 positions citywide, and a savings of $78M. For schools losing teachers, the gap is hard to fill.

→ Here’s an example:
Take a typical elementary school with around 600 students in FY26. Enrollment drops by roughly 50 in FY27. That means TWO fewer teaching positions. 

Add the ratio increase: The school received one teacher for every 24 students in FY26. They have one for every 25 in FY27. That’s likely the loss of a THIRD position.

Three teachers. That's the gap a principal will now have to try to fill. 

They can use discretionary funds to buy back a position, but those dollars were committed to something else in FY26: a literacy interventionist, after school programming, an additional social worker. 

Every buyback in FY27 is a subtraction somewhere else.

→ Aren’t there caps?
Yes. CPS capped losses at four teachers per elementary and six per high school. 

The cap matters, but it only applies to centrally allocated general education positions. Program cuts or shifting student needs can push losses beyond it.

→ A reminder about small schools

For the most part, the schools below the 250-student threshold did not face teacher cuts. However, these schools did lose their foundational assistant principal, an issue we’ll tackle tomorrow.
