Chicago Public Schools 2024–25 IAR Results: What the Data Show (and Don’t Show)

Last week, Chicago Public Schools (CPS) and the Illinois State Board of Education (ISBE) released the 2024–25 Illinois Assessment of Readiness (IAR) results — the statewide measure of student proficiency in reading and math. The data is available at the state, district, and school levels, disaggregated by demographic group.

Why this matters:
Statewide assessments help determine whether schools are providing students with the tools and environment they need to learn. In Illinois, they spotlight schools and districts achieving strong results — and illuminate opportunity gaps, helping direct resources where they’re needed most.

What’s different this year:
Under federal law, states must report the percentage of students in each achievement category, but they have discretion over the test and proficiency “cut scores.” For the 2024–25 school year, ISBE lowered those thresholds. Without access to the underlying scale scores, it’s impossible to track precise year-to-year changes — which is why we’re urging ISBE and CPS to release that data at the school level. (More on that next week!)

In the meantime, we can use the current data to explore key questions:
❓ Are our young people receiving the support they need to learn?
❓ Where are we seeing success?
❓ How can we expand those practices elsewhere?

Let’s start here: Are our young people receiving the support they need to learn?

CPS recalculated prior-year data using the lower proficiency thresholds and reported steady, though slowing, progress:
📘Reading (Grades 3–8): 28.7% (2022) → 34.3% (2023) → 40.0% (2024) → 40.6% (2025)
🧮Math (Grades 3–8): 21.1% (2022) → 24.4% (2023) → 25.5% (2024) → 26.2% (2025)

The bottom line:
Even with lower cut scores, only 4 in 10 CPS students meet reading proficiency standards — and fewer than 3 in 10 meet math benchmarks. Statewide, about 5 in 10 students are proficient in reading, and fewer than 4 in 10 in math.

Every family wants their child to be proficient in elementary reading and math. These skills are foundational for success in high school and beyond, as well as for navigating an increasingly information-rich world.

Meeting that goal takes focus, partnership, and persistence. The good news: we know it’s possible. Nineteen Chicago schools were recognized by ISBE as exemplary this year.

We’ll take a closer look at those stories and additional data points in the coming weeks.

FY27 Revenue Explainer #3: Local Property Taxes
CPS receives roughly $4B in property tax revenue annually.

In FY26, property tax revenue accounted for about 40% of the $10.25B total budget and 48% of the district's $9B operating budget. In Illinois, a school board’s power to increase a property tax levy is capped at 5% or the rate of inflation, whichever is less.

In December 2025, the Chicago Board of Education increased the levy by the maximum allowed: 2.9%. This generated roughly $73M in additional revenue for the FY26 budget. New property coming online and other shifts in the tax base added another $160M in new revenue for FY26.

This steady growth has helped CPS meet student needs, and the district has raised its levy to the cap for the last 15 years.

Another increase of around $240M, on par with FY26 growth, is expected in FY27. The total includes additional revenue from raising the cap and other increases in the tax base. The $240M is already assumed in the $520M deficit projected for FY27. 

Caps mean CPS can’t raise additional revenue from this source.

Bottom line: Property taxes remain the largest revenue source for all districts in Illinois, including CPS. In FY27, they will make a meaningful contribution to meeting the needs of Chicago’s students. But, even after significant new revenue, the $520M gap remains.

📌 Next: TIF surplus – a meaningful resource with long-term risks.

Recently, I shared one potential way to close the Chicago Public Schools' $529M budget gap: TIF. 

Last June, the city outlined a path that could help; it includes allowing TIF districts to expire and could eventually mean up to $300 million annually for CPS. That would narrow the structural gap over time. 

Of course, the gap for FY26 could also grow:

➡️ CPS could receive reduced revenue from the state ($2.6B in FY25) or the federal government ($1B in non-COVID funding in FY25).

➡️ CPS might also face pressure to reimburse the City of Chicago for a share of the Municipal Employees Annuity and Benefit Fund (MEABF).

What do you need to know about MEABF?

 📌 The total annual cost of the MEABF was $900M in FY25. 

📌 Beginning in FY17, a water/sewer tax helped the city fund this obligation. It generated $260M in revenue in FY25. Notably, the tax rate has remained stagnant since FY21.

📌 ~30% of the MEABF liability is attributed to CPS employees; however, under state law, the city is responsible for making all payments.

📌 The city requested that the CBOE reimburse some of this cost starting in FY21; the CBOE complied from FY21 through FY24, when CPS reimbursed the city $175M. 

📌 CPS did not receive any of the revenue from the water and sewer tax in any of those years.

In a tight fiscal environment, there are no easy options:

 🔁 Borrowing delays the problem.

 💰 Raising taxes is politically challenging for the city, especially with a recession looming.

 ✂️ Cutting $175M from CPS to make the reimbursement could impact classrooms; that’s the equivalent of 1,400 teacher positions.

These decisions are tough, and they matter. The consequences will be felt by students, educators, and communities citywide.

Elementary School Attendance in Chicago and Illinois: What the Data Tell Us (and What They Don’t)

Last week, we reviewed the recent IAR (elementary assessment) data. This week, let’s turn to something just as fundamental: attendance. We’ll examine the data to reveal how often both students and teachers are showing up in Chicago and across the state.

Why this matters
Attendance is the quiet engine of learning.
 ✅ When students have what they need to show up consistently, they build skills, confidence, and connection.
 ✅ When teachers are supported to be in the classroom daily, they build relationships, routines, and continuity.

When students or teachers need to miss school, classroom rhythm is disrupted, and learning suffers.

What’s changed since 2019
Throughout the 2010s, attendance among both elementary students and teachers in Illinois was relatively stable. COVID-19 changed that dramatically. Statewide absences reached record highs in 2020–21, and although the data indicate a recovery, we’re still not back to pre-pandemic norms.

Elementary Student Attendance (K–8)
Even with a gradual recovery, nearly one in three CPS elementary students misses more than 18 days in a typical 180-day school year.

Teacher Attendance Trends
The percentage of Chicago teachers missing more than 10 days per school year has also increased since 2018. We know that there is a correlation between teacher absences and student achievement, and that trust is built in classrooms over time. 

The bottom line
Teacher and student attendance build the ecosystem for trust and help foster learning. 

Patterns like these require time and attention to interrupt, but that investment pays off: when students, teachers, and families all have what they need to show up, learning flourishes.

Supporting young people and teachers begins with acknowledging that recovery is underway, albeit unevenly. Schools serving higher-need students continue to face deeper challenges tied to health, housing instability, transportation, and burnout. 

Addressing these trends requires connection — with educators, communities, families, and young people.

The good news
Some Chicago elementary schools are proving what’s possible.

Schools that have made the most significant gains in student attendance also report:
✅ Stronger teacher attendance
✅ More consistent communication with families, including home visits
✅ Targeted supports, from morning check-ins to transportation partnerships and “attendance champion” teams

The lesson is clear: showing up starts with feeling seen.

More to come on the bright spots across Chicago and Illinois, where both students and teachers are showing up and thriving every day.

FY27 Revenue Explainer #6: Recap

Over the past two weeks, I’ve reviewed CPS’s major revenue sources and their impact on the district’s financial outlook. 

To recap, CPS is likely to receive around $9B in operating revenue for FY27 from three sources:

🇺🇸 Federal: $900M (10%) in stable funding for major streams, but smaller grants can be cut with little warning.
🏛️ State: $2.4B (26%) in support; this includes $70M in growth through the Evidence-Based Finding Formula.
🏙️ Local: $5.7B (62%) in total, with roughly $240M secured in growth through increased property tax revenue, along with up to $552M assumed in TIF surplus, level with FY26 actual revenue and $173M over the FY26 budgeted amount. 

Summary: These three sources could yield nearly $500M in new revenue over FY26, resulting in a deficit of about $350M. 

But that number isn’t firm: In the FY26 budget book, CPS assumed closer to $300M in new revenue, including less in TIF surplus. CPS projected a $520M+ gap relative to projected expenses at that time.

At this stage in the budget cycle, there is no room for additional growth through federal, state, or property tax sources. 

TIF surpluses could grow, but the city decides as late as December, too late for the CPS budget decisions underway now.

Bottom line: Principals will learn how much of the gap will be absorbed in their schools as they receive their school budgets, likely next week. When those budgets hit, I’ll dive into what cuts could mean for Chicago schools and students.

FY27 Revenue Explainer #4: Tax Increment Financing Districts (TIF)

In FY26, CPS received $552M from TIF surpluses. That is about 5% of the $10.25B total budget, and 6% of the district’s $8.7B operating budget, a small but meaningful share.

⁉️ How do those dollars come to CPS?

Tax Increment Financing (TIF) is an economic development tool that sets aside increases in property tax revenue to fund redevelopment projects within a specific geographic area.

Taxing bodies, like CPS, don’t receive the incremental increases for the period the TIF is active, generally 23 years.

⌚ Over time, TIF districts may generate more property tax revenue than needed for planned projects. When that happens, state law requires the unused funds to be surplused. 

By law, CPS receives about 52% of the total. In 2019, the City of Chicago adopted a formal policy to declare surplus. In FY26, the City declared a surplus of over $1B, and CPS received $552M:

▶️ $397M ◀️ 
▪️Available to cover operating expenses for CPS, slightly above the $379M assumed in the budget CPS passed.

▶️$175M ◀️ 
▪️Returned as reimbursement to the City for Municipal Employees Annuity & Benefit Fund (MEABF) costs, per the district’s agreement with the City.

⏸️ Here's the catch. ⏸️ 

The City is not required to finalize the TIF surplus until December. CPS must pass its budget by August. That's a real calendar challenge, and it makes TIF funding risky to calculate and to count on.

What’s more, the amount available varies from year-to-year. Even with a formal process, politics often come into play. Counting on TIF dollars for steady-state operations is not a sustainable, long-term strategy.

📣 Bottom line: TIF surpluses are politically-dependent, variable in amount, and -- by design -- one-time sources of revenue. The total amount is only known after the CPS budget is passed. Still, we CAN make some plausible assumptions based on previous years, which we’ll do in the next post.

As Nelson Gerew highlighted in his recent testimony before the Illinois House Executive Committee, Chicago Public Schools (CPS) has made real progress since the passage of the Evidence-Based Funding (EBF) formula in 2017. State revenue has grown, local revenue has increased, and COVID relief dollars allowed for real gains in student learning.

But as those federal funds expire, CPS is once again facing structural deficits. Tomorrow’s Board of Education vote will close a $734M gap for FY26. That is necessary work, but it is only the beginning.

To ensure long-term stability for CPS — and fairness for students across Illinois — we need state-level solutions. Four stand out:

✅ Accelerate the path to adequacy. At $350M per year, Illinois won’t reach adequacy until the 2030s. CPS, which just moved from Tier 2 to Tier 1 in the EBF formula, is currently at 73% adequacy — meaning its 325,000+ students receive only 79 cents on the dollar for what they need. Chicago is not alone: students in Rockford, East St. Louis, and dozens of other districts cannot afford to wait another decade.

✅ Fully fund special education. CPS has nearly doubled the number of special education classroom assistants since 2019 — a critical investment for equity and inclusion. But the state formula does not keep pace with the true cost of serving students with disabilities. Updating EBF to reflect actual special education needs would provide a lifeline for families across Illinois.

✅ Share responsibility for teacher pensions. CPS legacy pension costs exceed $650M annually, requiring the district to divert over $100M from its operating budget each year. Expanding state support, beyond just the “normal cost,” would free up local resources to directly benefit students.

✅ Enable local revenue options. CPS raises 60% of its budget through property taxes, but it is capped at inflation or 5%. Without authority to issue levies beyond existing caps, CPS has little ability to respond to crises or sustain investments that work. State flexibility here could prevent mid-year cuts and layoffs like those seen a decade ago.

The lesson from Nelson’s testimony is clear: when Chicago and Illinois have invested in schools, students have delivered. CPS eighth-graders now outperform national averages in reading. Graduation rates are rising, and more graduates are leaving with college credit and AP scores than ever before.

Tomorrow’s CPS budget is step one. Step two must be an urgent, statewide conversation about adequacy, equity, and sustainability. Illinois has shown before that bipartisan solutions are possible. Our students deserve nothing less.

FY27 Revenue Explainer 5: TIF Surplus Assumptions - Part 2 ⤵️ 

Yesterday, I explained how TIF surpluses factored into the CPS budget in FY26 and why they aren’t as predictable as CPS’s other revenue sources. Today, we’ll consider how much CPS is likely to receive in FY27.

💡 To start, it’s important to remember that as TIF districts age, their property values grow. Over time, the tax revenue they generate may exceed the amount required by their planned redevelopment projects. 

When these funds are declared surplus, CPS receives about 52% of that amount. In the last four years, the declared surplus has grown steadily.

📊 TIF surplus declared - City of Chicago
▪️$395M > FY23
▪️$435M > FY24
▪️$712M > FY25 
▪️$1.01B > FY26

Even as the surpluses have grown, the total TIF balance has remained high. This means that - while the surpluses are substantial - the overall revenue available for development projects remains high. Balances have been increasing even after these surplus declarations!

📊TIF balance, as of December 31
▪️$2.5B > 2022
▪️$3.1B > 2023 
▪️$3.2B > 2024 
▪️$3.3B > 2025

Based on this information, it seems safe to assume that the FY27 TIF surplus declaration will be similar to FY26's: $552M.

The current deficit projection of $520M assumes only $379M in TIF surplus. If CPS received $552M without conditions around the MEABF, the budget gap would shrink to $375M.

Of course, that assumption is not a guarantee. CPS and the City will discuss projections in the coming weeks, and the CBOE will need to decide how much TIF surplus to assume in the budget they pass this summer.

📣Bottom line: CPS could assume up to $552M in TIF surplus in FY27, helping close the projected gap. But, even that wouldn’t be enough.

CPS receives roughly $4B in property tax revenue annually. 

That’s about 40% of the $10.25B total budget, and nearly half of the district's $8.6B operating budget. In Illinois, a school board’s power to increase a property tax levy is capped at 5% or the rate of inflation, whichever is less.

In December 2025, the Chicago Board of Education increased the levy by the maximum allowed: 2.9%. This generated roughly $73M in additional revenue for the FY26 budget. New property coming online and other shifts in the tax base added another $100M in new revenue for FY26.

This steady growth has helped CPS meet growing student needs, which is why the district has raised its levy to the cap for the last 13 years. 

Another increase is already assumed in the $500M+ deficit projected for FY27. Caps mean additional revenue won't come from this source.

Bottom line: Property taxes remain the largest revenue source for all districts in Illinois, including CPS. In FY27, they will make a meaningful contribution to meeting Chicago’s students' needs. But, even after significant new revenue, the $500M+ gap remains.

High School Assessment Results: What the 2024–25 Data Tells Us

ISBE and CPS released new performance data this fall, and one trend is clear: college-readiness is slipping—locally and nationally. No single test tells the whole story, but the pattern is unmistakable.

Chicago, once a national outlier for improvement, is now experiencing a slower version of the same nationwide slide. The question isn’t whether the trend is real—it’s how quickly we can reverse it.

How High School Assessment Works in Illinois
Illinois has long used a college-readiness exam for its statewide test, moving from ACT → SAT → ACT again in 2025. Due to this shift, year-to-year comparisons are challenging, but the long-term trend is clear.

📉 The Trend
In 2025, CPS 11th graders averaged 17.1 (Math) and 16.6 (ELA) on the ACT—down 1.2 points from a decade ago.

CPS SAT scores also declined steadily, from 969 (2018) to 929 (2024).
Notably, some outcomes continue to rise—graduation rates and early college credentials among them. Historically, CPS improved these alongside test scores. A decade-long decline is unusual.

National data mirrors the pattern: ACT math averages fell from 20.8 → 18.9, and ELA from 20.9 → 19.2 since 2015.

Where Do We Go From Here?
Reversing the slide—and returning to the steady progress Chicago once led—will require:
- Stronger early high school reading and math supports
- A deep focus on high-quality instruction and rigorous curriculum
- Transparent, ongoing monitoring of multiple data points—not just ACT results

Chicago has proven that improvement is possible. The challenge now is to ensure that rising graduation and credential rates are matched by genuine academic readiness. Every student deserves to leave high school prepared for what comes next.

State funding is increasing each year, but most districts statewide still do not receive the funding necessary to meet the needs of the students they serve.

BOTTOM LINE: Annual increases in state revenue help CPS get closer to a balanced budget, but aren’t yet enough to fully meet student needs. In SY27, the additional dollars will make a difference, but won’t close the gap.

📉 Chicago Public Schools’ (CPS) $734 million deficit includes a proposed $175 million reimbursement payment to the City of Chicago for the Municipal Employees Annuity and Benefit Fund (MEABF).

This pension system covers CPS employees who are not certified educators. Importantly, CPS is not legally obligated to make this payment, and for nearly 100 years, it did not. Between 2020 and 2023, the district reimbursed the city using one-time federal COVID-19 relief funds, but those dollars are no longer available. Covering this cost now would mean either cuts to the CPS budget or additional borrowing.

Public opinion reflects skepticism as only 25% of voters support CPS taking on this responsibility.

💡How can CPS and the city of Chicago resolve the MEABF payment situation? Well, some potential solutions include:
▪️ A new, dedicated tax levy authorized by the state
▪️ State absorption of CPS’s normal pension costs for these employees, as it already does for teachers
▪️ The city of Chicago owning the cost of MEABF without expecting any contribution from CPS (at least until the district fixes its structural budget deficit)

Any path forward will require collaboration between CPS, the city of Chicago, and state leaders. What remains clear: addressing this obligation without new revenue would come at a significant cost to students.
